title: Targeted search: finding the clients that fit your service for Handyman
audience: Handyman owners who want more repeat visits from property managers, real estate offices, strata managers and public bodies in their own service area.
learningOutcomes: Build a prospect list scored against written fit criteria for service area, visit size and repeat need
Identify public signals that a maintenance need is starting, and explain why each one is a reasonable reason to make contact
Write a first approach that makes one specific, verifiable observation, offers one small next step and can be declined easily

instruction.heading: Decide what work you want before you look for it
instruction.body: Write down the visit types you do well, the suburbs you can reach without losing money on travel, the visit size you can sustain, and how often each kind of client needs you. A fortnightly maintenance round on a route you already run is usually worth more to a handyman than a single job across town. These criteria are the filter for everything that follows. Without them, a lead cannot be judged.

instruction.heading: Build a scored prospect list
instruction.body: Keep every candidate in one list with a fit column, a status column, a source and a date added. Score each one as strong fit, possible fit or not a fit. Ask whether it sits inside your service area, whether it has a repeat need for small tasks, such as a rental portfolio, a strata common area or a holiday rental, whether you can reach the person who decides, and whether the work sits inside your licence and insurance. Property managers, real estate offices and strata managers are candidates to test. No source in this course's research shows how often these clients buy handyman work, so treat each group as a hypothesis. A vendor legal-blog says many clients and strata managers will not let a tradesperson on site without insurance. That is a vendor view, not client-acquisition evidence. Use only business contact details published for business use. Buying a list does not remove the need to show consent, according to ACMA.

instruction.heading: Watch public signals
instruction.body: In Victoria, Buying for Victoria lists current and past tenders, lets suppliers set alerts, and publishes each agency's annual plan of what it intends to buy. AusTender does the same for federal work. Some councils publish planning permit registers, such as the City of Casey register in Victoria's open data portal. Use signals to decide when to contact a business or public body, not to build a profile of individuals. Do not monitor private people, use personal information that is not public, enter private property, or turn up at a home to make an offer.

instruction.heading: Make a first approach that is specific and easy to decline
instruction.body: A useful first message says how you came to know about the need, makes one specific observation that you can verify from public view or the business's own published material, and offers one small next step, such as a written quote for a defined list or a fifteen-minute call. The ACCC's July 2026 release on unsolicited selling reported that many approaches were pressured or misleading, and that about 71 per cent of salespeople identified themselves. An honest, named approach therefore stands out.

instruction.heading: Follow up on a fixed schedule and stop when asked
instruction.body: Decide the follow-ups in advance. A common pattern is one reminder after a week and one final message two weeks later, then a pause. If a prospect says no or asks you to stop, remove them at once and record the request with its date. At the end of each month, review which fit tier and which signal produced the replies that became paid work.

procedure: Write the visit types, area, size and repeat-need criteria for the work you want.
Build the prospect list and score each entry as strong fit, possible fit or not a fit, with a reason and a source.
Choose two or three public signals to watch and record the date each one is seen.
Write one first message for each fit tier, with a stated source, one verifiable observation and one small next step.
Check each message against the electronic message rules and the licence rules for the work before sending.
Send to strong-fit prospects first, then follow up on the fixed schedule.
Remove anyone who asks you to stop, and review the results at the end of the month.

workedExamples.situation: A handyman covers three suburbs in Victoria. A public tender notice appears on Buying for Victoria for minor maintenance at a public facility in one of them, with a closing date and a named contact for questions. The scenario is illustrative.
workedExamples.decisionPrompt: Should the handyman respond, and what should the response contain?
workedExamples.reasoning: The tender is a public route the agency has opened, so responding through the stated process is appropriate. Before he responds, he confirms the scope, his capacity and the deadline, which Business Queensland advises before any quote, even though it is a Queensland source applied here as general practice. He checks that each task is inside the licence and insurance he holds in Victoria. The Victorian licence position for some trade tasks is not settled in the research, so he checks it with the regulator. He does not contact individual staff using private contact details. His response names the tender, says how he found it, offers one defined set of tasks with a price basis, and asks one question about access. He does not pressure the agency.

equipmentAndPpe: Prospect list in a spreadsheet or notebook, with fit, status, source and date columns
Written fit criteria for service area, visit size and repeat need
Message templates checked against the electronic message rules
No PPE is needed for desk work; any site visit follows the site's own safety rules

commonErrors.error: Sending the same message to everyone on a broad list at once.
commonErrors.prevention: Score the list first, write one message for each fit tier, and start with the strong-fit tier.

commonErrors.error: Using private information about an individual to make contact.
commonErrors.prevention: Use only contact details published for business use, or details the person has given you for this purpose.

commonErrors.error: Pitching a licensed trade task that you are not licensed or insured to do.
commonErrors.prevention: Check the licence and insurance before outreach, and remove that task from the message.

commonErrors.error: Following up without a limit, or continuing after a request to stop.
commonErrors.prevention: Set a fixed number of follow-ups and a stop rule, and record every stop request.

safetyAndRegulatory.point: Do not offer a licensed trade task in outreach unless you hold the licence that the state where the work is done requires. Queensland and NSW thresholds differ, and the Victorian licence position for some handyman tasks is unresolved in the research. Check the rule for each state before you pitch. This lesson does not grant any licence.

Commercial electronic messages, including email and text, are regulated by the Spam Act 2003 (Cth). ACMA's guidance says marketing messages need consent, that consent should be recorded, and that unsubscribe requests must be honoured within five working days. ACMA's Spam Act obligations page (last updated 28 March 2019) says publishing a business address does not by itself permit commercial messages. The Act text was not read for this lesson.

A public listing or public notice does not by itself permit contact about anything. If the Privacy Act applies to your business, the OAIC's direct-marketing guidance says public information is not exempt. Whether it applies to a small handyman business is not settled in the research, so check it. Use only contact details published for business use, keep them secure, and stop when someone objects.

Telemarketing to numbers on the Do Not Call Register is limited to weekdays from 9 am to 8 pm and Saturdays from 9 am to 5 pm, and not on Sundays or public holidays. That is from a 2018 industry guide, so check for updates before calling.

qualityStandard: Every prospect on the list has a fit score, a reason for that score and a recorded source for its contact details.
Every first message contains one verifiable observation and one small, easy-to-decline next step.
No contact is made using private information, and every stop request is recorded and actioned.
documentationEvidence: Prospect list with fit score, reason, status, source and date added
Signal log with the date each public signal was seen
Stop-request record with the date it was actioned
summary: Define the work you want first, then filter prospects against that definition.
Watch public signals, and never use private information to make contact.
Keep the first approach specific and easy to decline, and stop when asked.

knowledgeChecks.question: Which prospect should you contact first?
options: Any business that has a website, because it probably spends money on services
A one-off job well outside your service area, because it looks large
A property group with several sites inside your service area that you already visit

knowledgeChecks.question: A public notice shows planned maintenance at a building in your area. What is the most appropriate first step?
options: Message each resident using their private contact details
Contact the building's manager through a route that the electronic message and Do Not Call rules allow
Go into the common area to look at the work before making contact

knowledgeChecks.question: Before you send a commercial email to a prospect, what should you do?
options: Ask the prospect to like your social media page first
Choose a fun subject line and keep the message short
Confirm the Spam Act 2003 requirements in current ACMA guidance before sending
